inserts.title: Moving electrodes capture spikes during behavior
paragraphs: A microdrive moves the electrode in small steps, so a single unit can be followed as the rat changes behavior. Walking, grooming, eating and resting were all observed during the same recording session, so each spike train is paired with the behavior it accompanies.

Differential recording subtracts the signal shared by two nearby electrodes. That subtraction reduced artifacts from muscle and movement, which let the spikes of the hippocampal unit stand out during free movement. Both signals were recorded at one electrode site, so every spike is tied to the tissue it came from.

The authors also presented sounds, moving visual stimuli, odors and touch to the same units. Responses to these stimuli separated spatially dependent firing from ordinary sensory responsiveness. Each stimulus type was presented while the same unit was recorded, so the responses can be compared directly.

inserts.title: Light removal abolishes a touch-evoked response
paragraphs: Turning off the lights removed the response of the featured CA1 unit. The restricted tactile response therefore depended on visual information, even though touch on the animal's back was the stimulus that evoked the firing. The stimulus that evoked the firing was touch, which shows that a visual condition can gate a tactile response.

Moving striped cards produced no response that a small visual receptive field could explain. A receptive field is the region of sensory space in which a suitable stimulus changes a neuron's activity, and the result pointed to the wider surrounding view. The striped cards were moved through the visual field, so features across that whole field were tested.

The rat turned through several effective orientations, so a fixed retinal image is an unlikely explanation. The observations favored dependence on the surrounding visual configuration over any single landmark. The surrounding visual configuration offered a stable reference as the rat rotated through its orientations.

inserts.title: The cognitive map links firing to predicted input
paragraphs: O'Keefe and Dostrovsky proposed that spatially selective cells, together with movement signals, could recruit cells representing subsequent orientations. In this model the network anticipates the sensory input that movement brings. The model describes a sequence in which each population prepares the next orientation before the animal moves.

The 1971 recordings established location-dependent firing. Prediction, route selection and the explanation of lesion-induced deficits were extensions that the authors built on those recordings. Route selection and lesion effects were therefore predictions that depended on the recorded spatial responses.

A neural representation is a reliable link between activity and a variable. A navigational mechanism adds transformations that guide behavior, and testing that mechanism calls for circuit manipulations during tasks that require spatial choices. Tests of the model require recordings during tasks that place the animal at spatial decision points.

inserts.title: Occupancy correction sets the firing-rate scale
paragraphs: Hafting and colleagues recorded spikes while rats explored a circular arena, and the animals spent unequal time at each location. The firing rate at each location relates the spike count to the time the animal spent there. The analysis corrects for uneven exploration so that the rate at each location is a fair measure of firing.

Repeated regions of elevated rate remained after occupancy was built into the analysis. The repeated pattern therefore reflects where the cell fires, not where the rat lingers. The repeated elevated regions after this correction show that the pattern reflects the cell's firing.

Locations sampled poorly give little information about firing, so the reliability of each rate value depends on how thoroughly the arena was explored. A color map of these rates displays measured activity across the whole arena. The correction is applied to each location separately, so every part of the arena contributes its own rate.

inserts.title: Cross-correlation reveals a phase offset
paragraphs: Spatial cross-correlation compares two neurons' rate maps as one map slides across the other. A peak away from the origin marks the displacement that aligns the two firing patterns. Each shift of one map relative to the other produces a value, and the peaks identify the best alignments.

Neighboring grid cells shared spacing and orientation, yet their nearest peaks were offset from the origin. That offset measures the difference in spatial phase between the two cells. The peak offset is a quantitative value for phase, computed from the two rate maps in the same units.

Cells at different recording sites have different scales and orientations, so their cross-correlations are less sharply aligned. Shared inputs can produce a correlated pattern without any direct synapse between the recorded cells. The measure is useful because it reports the phase relation between two cells without needing a physical lattice.

inserts.title: Grid firing remains in the dark
paragraphs: Hafting and colleagues recorded a grid cell across 10 min of light, 10 min of darkness and a return to light. The animal stayed in the same environment throughout the session. The cell's firing was recorded in each light condition, so the three segments can be compared within one session.

The grid pattern persisted in darkness, although its fields became somewhat dispersed or displaced. Self-motion signals, which come from the animal's own movement, stay available when visual landmarks are removed. The fields in darkness stayed periodic and recognizable, even though their positions shifted somewhat.

Persistence without vision fits movement-based updating of location. Odors, touch and boundaries remain available, so self-motion is one of several inputs that can drive the pattern in darkness. The animal's self-motion therefore supplies information that persists when the visual scene is removed.

paragraphs: An interneuron is a neuron whose principal connections stay within a local circuit. Giocomo and colleagues compared theta-modulated entorhinal interneurons with the principal grid cells. Interneurons are inhibitory cells in many circuits, and their timing is a sensitive readout of network state.

The increase in theta timing was present in grid cells but was not comparably detected in simultaneously recorded interneurons. The change therefore concerns grid cells specifically, rather than every recorded neuron. The interneurons were recorded at the same time as the grid cells, so the timing is measured within the same session.

Cell-class differences constrain how a molecular intervention reshapes network dynamics. 3: An **extracellular recording** measures voltage changes outside neurons when they fire action potentials. A lightweight skull-mounted microdrive let electrodes advance through the dorsal hippocampus while the recovered rat walked, groomed, ate or remained still, so the spikes were recorded during natural behavior. The electrode could be moved between recording sessions, so the same tissue was sampled over time.

Adjacent recording and reference electrodes fed a differential amplifier, which reduced shared muscle and movement artifacts. At higher arousal, weak responses became possible outside the preferred orientation, while the preferred response grew stronger. **Arousal** here refers to the animal's behavioral activation state, which changed how readily sensory input produced spikes. They also removed prominent sound sources and darkened or occluded parts of the visual environment while monitoring spatially restricted responses. 11: **Histology** identifies tissue structure in thin stained brain sections. The recording location in Hafting and colleagues' example was in layer II of medial entorhinal cortex, near its border with postrhinal cortex. A **Nissl stain** highlights neuronal cell bodies and reveals cortical layers and regional boundaries. Electrode positions were reconstructed from their tracks and the recorded progression of the microdrive, linking physiological measurements to anatomical location.
